props.title: Chelsea Girls
props.initialSlug: Warhol's raw portrait of NYC underground life

sections.content: Chelsea Girls (1966) revolutionized experimental cinema through its groundbreaking split-screen presentation and 3.5-hour runtime. Andy Warhol and Paul Morrissey's provocative film captures the raw essence of New York's underground scene, filming various residents of the Chelsea Hotel in unscripted vignettes. Its influence echoes through later dual-projection works like Timecode (2000) and shaped the aesthetic of music documentaries like Don't Look Back (1967). The film's unflinching portrayal of sexuality, drug use, and bohemian life challenged censorship boundaries and established Warhol as a serious filmmaker beyond his pop art fame.

sections.content: The Factory scene that produced Chelsea Girls birthed a whole movement of experimental filmmaking. Flesh (1968) and Trash (1970), both directed by Paul Morrissey under Warhol's umbrella, continued pushing boundaries with their frank sexuality and drug imagery. The improvisational approach influenced John Cassavetes' style, particularly in Faces (1968), while the duration and patience of Warhol's lens inspired structural filmmakers like Michael Snow's Wavelength (1967).

Chelsea Girls' technical innovation of simultaneous projection created a template for expanded cinema. The Clock (2010) by Christian Marclay and Ragnar Kjartansson's The Visitors (2012) build on its multi-screen legacy in gallery spaces. The film's documentation of queer underground culture laid groundwork for later works like Paris Is Burning (1990) and Portrait of Jason (1967). SUBHEAD: Impact on Underground Cinema

sections.content: The reverberations of Chelsea Girls' DIY aesthetic influenced generations of no-budget filmmakers. Permanent Vacation (1980), Jim Jarmusch's debut, channels its loose narrative and urban decay imagery. Jonas Mekas, who championed Chelsea Girls, created Walden: Diaries, Notes and Sketches (1969) using similar documentary techniques. The film's frank treatment of marginalized communities inspired later underground auteurs like Nick Zedd and Richard Kern in the Cinema of Transgression movement.
